stem: A project has test files distributed across multiple subdirectories alongside source code. The team wants uniform testing conventions to apply automatically whenever Claude Code works on test files, without loading those conventions during unrelated edits. What is the recommended configuration?

options.text: Add nested CLAUDE.md files in every test subdirectory instructing Claude Code to inspect neighboring source files.
Define a custom slash command in .claude/commands/ that runs an interactive linter check before every write operation.
Create rule files in .claude/rules/ with YAML frontmatter specifying paths glob patterns matching the test files.
Configure the root CLAUDE.md file with an @include-glob directive pointing to the workspace test configuration file.

explanation: Rule files placed in .claude/rules/ support YAML frontmatter with a paths field containing glob patterns (such as **/*.test.ts). Claude Code conditionally loads these rules only when Claude reads matching files, ensuring conventions apply across all directories without bloating context for non-test tasks.

distractorNotes.a: Subdirectory CLAUDE.md files do not scale when test files are distributed throughout dozens of folders.
distractorNotes.b: Slash commands require manual invocation and do not provide automatic convention loading during edits.
distractorNotes.d: CLAUDE.md supports @import for file inclusion, but does not support an @include-glob directive for path matching.

sourceNote: Path-specific rules in .claude/rules/ using YAML frontmatter paths glob patterns

stem: A tech lead establishes coding conventions for a microservices repository so that all contributors and automated pipelines adhere to identical linting and style rules. Newly onboarded engineers clone the repository and find that Claude Code ignores the conventions completely, while the lead's own local sessions follow them without issue. Which configuration mistake causes this discrepancy?

options.text: The lead placed the conventions in a nested folder, and Claude Code requires every engineer to run claude init to link project memory.
The new engineers have user-scoped ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md files that take precedence and completely override project-level memory.
The lead configured the conventions using path-specific rules in .claude/rules/, which are not shared across git checkouts by default.
The conventions were saved in the lead's user-scoped ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md rather than committed to a project-level CLAUDE.md in version control.

explanation: User-scoped memory at ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md applies only to the individual developer's machine and is never shared through git. For repository conventions to apply automatically to all contributors upon checkout, they must be committed to a project-level CLAUDE.md (or .claude/rules/) within the repository root.

distractorNotes.a: Claude Code does not require a manual init command to read project memory; it automatically discovers CLAUDE.md files in the current repository.
distractorNotes.b: User-scoped memory loads before project-scoped memory and both are concatenated; user-scoped memory does not override or suppress project-level files.
distractorNotes.c: Files committed under .claude/rules/ in the repository are tracked by git and available to all developers immediately upon checkout.

sourceNote: Distinguishing user-scoped ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md from project-scoped CLAUDE.md

stem: A monorepo contains several distinct packages maintained by different squads. The team wants to keep the root CLAUDE.md concise while importing specialized package standards maintained in separate files. What mechanism should be used?

options.text: Use the `@path/to/import` syntax (for example `@./packages/billing/CLAUDE.md`) inside the project markdown configuration.
Use standard Markdown link syntax [Billing Standards](./packages/billing/CLAUDE.md) to instruct Claude Code to inline the file at launch.
Add each package's CLAUDE.md path to a 'memory' array in the repository's package.json so Claude Code loads them at startup.
Launch Claude Code with --add-dir packages/billing so that package's CLAUDE.md is pulled into the root session alongside the root file.

explanation: Claude Code supports modular memory through the `@path/to/import` syntax in CLAUDE.md files: `@` followed by a path inlines that file. This enables referencing external markdown files across packages or documentation trees, keeping the root memory clean and maintainable while pulling in domain-specific standards. Imports resolve recursively to a maximum depth of four hops, and import parsing skips Markdown code spans and fenced code blocks.

distractorNotes.b: Standard Markdown links [label](path) are rendered as regular link text and do not inline file contents into the context window; an `@path` import line is required.
distractorNotes.c: package.json is not part of Claude Code memory resolution; specialized files are pulled in with an `@path` import line inside the markdown, not a package.json array.
distractorNotes.d: --add-dir grants access to additional directories, but by default CLAUDE.md files from those directories are not loaded (that needs CLAUDE_CODE_ADDITIONAL_DIRECTORIES_CLAUDE_MD); an `@path` import line in the root CLAUDE.md is the import mechanism.

sourceNote: Import additional files — `@path/to/import` syntax for modular, maintainable CLAUDE.md configurations

stem: A monolithic CLAUDE.md file has expanded to over 4,000 lines, covering frontend styling, database migration rules, Docker setup, and API security. Developers notice slower startup and frequent token waste on unrelated tasks. What is the recommended architectural remedy?

options.text: Move the conventions into individual developer CLAUDE.local.md files so the shared project CLAUDE.md file stays under 50 lines.
Split the monolithic file into focused topic files inside .claude/rules/ (e.g. testing.md, db.md) using conditional path scoping where appropriate.
Move the entire 4,000-line file into a system prompt via settings so it loads once and is cached, rather than keeping it as CLAUDE.md.
Keep the single file but wrap each section in HTML comments so Claude Code skips the irrelevant sections automatically.

explanation: Monolithic memory files inflate context windows and consume tokens regardless of task relevance. Decomposing instructions into topic-specific files under `.claude/rules/`—and leveraging YAML frontmatter paths to conditionally load them only when editing relevant files—keeps context focused and reduces overhead.

distractorNotes.a: CLAUDE.local.md is intended for personal user-specific overrides and is meant to be gitignored, making it incapable of maintaining shared team standards.
distractorNotes.c: Relocating the same 4,000 lines into a system prompt still injects all of it every turn; the remedy is splitting into focused, path-scoped topic files so only relevant rules load.
distractorNotes.d: Block-level HTML comments are stripped before CLAUDE.md is injected, so wrapped sections would be dropped for every task rather than loaded when relevant; conditional path scoping across separate rule files is what limits what loads.

sourceNote: Splitting monolithic CLAUDE.md files into topic-specific rule files in .claude/rules/

stem: An engineer working in a complex monorepo suspects that conflicting memory instructions from ancestor directories are degrading Claude Code's responses during file edits. The engineer needs to verify exactly which CLAUDE.md and rules files have been loaded into the active session context. What is the proper command?

options.text: Run /doctor, whose setup checkup lists the memory files and rules files that are active in the current session.
Run /context, which visualizes what is filling the context window and reports the CLAUDE.md and rules files that were loaded into the session.
Run /memory, which lists the memory files loaded for the session and lets the engineer open any of them to inspect the active instructions.
Run /status, whose session rows report which memory files and rules were loaded when the session started.

explanation: The exam guide's skill for this objective is verifying which memory files are loaded with `/memory`, which lists the memory files in scope for the session and opens any of them for inspection. `/doctor` runs a setup checkup (installation health, PATH, settings, unused skills and MCP servers, CLAUDE.md dedup), `/status` reports version, model, account and connectivity, and `/context` visualizes context usage. Divergence recorded in review-progress.md: current `memory.md` says to check the Memory files list under `/context` and describes `/memory` as listing file locations, including files that do not exist yet; the exam guide names `/memory`, so that is the key here.

distractorNotes.a: /doctor is a setup checkup: it diagnoses installation and configuration health, flags unused skills, MCP servers and plugins, and can deduplicate or trim CLAUDE.md files. It does not report which memory files the current session loaded.
distractorNotes.b: The near miss: current `memory.md` points at `/context` for this check and its Memory files list does show loaded CLAUDE.md and rules files. The exam guide's task statement names `/memory` as the command that verifies which memory files are loaded, so `/context` is the trap. (Divergence recorded in review-progress.md.)
distractorNotes.d: /status opens the Settings interface on the Status tab, showing version, model, account and connectivity. It carries no per-session inventory of memory files.

sourceNote: Exam Guide v1.0 § Task Statement 3.1 — /memory verifies which memory files are loaded

stem: A team wants to define a custom slash command /e2e-check that runs end-to-end regression tests and generates a summary. All developers on the project should have access to it immediately upon git pull. Where must the command file be placed?

options.text: In ~/.claude/commands/e2e-check.md on the lead developer's machine, relying on background cloud synchronization across accounts.
Inside the root package.json under a 'slashCommands' key configured with raw bash execution scripts for pipeline automation.
Committed to the repository root as e2e-check.md alongside the README, where Claude Code auto-discovers top-level command files.
In the project repository under .claude/commands/e2e-check.md

explanation: Project-scoped custom slash commands are stored in `.claude/commands/` within the repository root. When committed to git, any team member who pulls the repository gets the custom command automatically available in their Claude Code sessions.

distractorNotes.a: Files placed in ~/.claude/commands/ are user-scoped and not shared through project git repositories.
distractorNotes.b: Claude Code does not parse package.json for custom slash command definitions.
distractorNotes.c: Claude Code resolves project slash commands from .claude/commands/ (or .claude/skills/), not from arbitrary top-level markdown files; placing it at the repo root does not register the command.

sourceNote: Project-scoped custom slash commands in .claude/commands/ for version-controlled team sharing

stem: An engineer authors a custom skill in .claude/skills/audit-architecture/SKILL.md that performs extensive codebase exploration, reading dozens of files and generating lengthy diagnostic trees. What frontmatter configuration prevents this exploratory context from polluting the main conversation?

options.text: context: fork, which executes the skill in an isolated subagent context and returns only the final response to the main session.
background: true, which runs the skill as a background task so its exploration stays out of the main conversation.
output: silent, which suppresses all intermediate tool call outputs and file reading tokens from being appended to the transcript.
disable-model-invocation: true, which keeps the skill's exploration out of the main conversation until a developer invokes it explicitly.

explanation: Setting `context: fork` in a skill's YAML frontmatter instructs Claude Code to run the skill inside an isolated sub-agent context. The exploratory reading and voluminous intermediate outputs remain confined to the fork, and only the final synthesis is returned to the main conversation.

distractorNotes.b: The background field applies only together with context: fork; on its own it does not isolate anything. The isolation comes from context: fork, which runs the skill in a forked subagent context.
distractorNotes.c: 'output: silent' is an invented property; suppressing exploration tokens from polluting the main conversation is achieved via 'context: fork'.
distractorNotes.d: disable-model-invocation controls who can invoke the skill (it stops Claude from loading it automatically); once invoked, the skill still runs in the main conversation. Isolation requires context: fork.

sourceNote: Using context: fork frontmatter to isolate verbose skill execution from main conversation context

stem: A skill is created to generate architectural documentation. To ensure that invoking this skill cannot inadvertently modify or delete source code files while it runs, how should the skill frontmatter be configured?

options.text: Instruct Claude in the skill text: 'Please do not edit files, we strictly forbid any write operations during this task.'
Configure allowed-tools with only read and search tools (Read, Grep, Glob), restricting the skill to those tools and withholding Write and Edit while it runs.
Add a hook that runs after each Edit or Write and reverts the changes the skill makes to source files.
List Write, Edit and Bash in disallowed-tools, which removes them from Claude's tool pool while the skill is active.

explanation: The exam guide's skill for this objective is configuring `allowed-tools` in skill frontmatter to restrict tool access during skill execution, leaving the write-capable tools out so the skill cannot modify or delete source. The other options do not deliver that: a prompt-level prohibition is probabilistic, and a revert-after-write hook lets the write land before undoing it. `disallowed-tools` is the near miss — the field current `skills.md` documents for removing tools from the pool while a skill is active — but the exam guide names `allowed-tools` for this objective, which is what the item keys. Divergence recorded in review-progress.md: current `skills.md` says `allowed-tools` pre-approves the tools it lists without restricting which are available.

distractorNotes.a: Prompt instructions are probabilistic and do not offer deterministic security guarantees.
distractorNotes.c: A revert-after-write hook lets the write happen and undoes it afterwards, so the skill still reaches the source files; the frontmatter has to determine what the skill can use.
distractorNotes.d: The near miss: current `skills.md` documents `disallowed-tools` as the field that removes tools from Claude's pool while a skill is active. The blueprint's task statement names `allowed-tools` as the frontmatter configuration that restricts tool access during skill execution, which is what this item tests. (Divergence recorded in review-progress.md.)

sourceNote: Exam Guide v1.0 § Task Statement 3.2 — allowed-tools frontmatter restricts tool access during skill execution

stem: A DevOps team creates a custom slash command /deploy-check in .claude/skills/deploy-check/SKILL.md that takes an issue key (e.g. /deploy-check JIRA-101). Developers frequently invoke it without the required argument. Which frontmatter configuration prompts developers for the required parameter when the skill is invoked without it?

options.text: arguments: '[ticket-number]', which declares the skill's positional argument and prompts for its value when developers omit it.
when_to_use: 'invoke with ticket number', which prompts for the missing argument by describing the expected invocation in the skill listing.
argument-hint: '[ticket-number]', the frontmatter field for prompting developers for the required parameter when they invoke the skill without it.
disable-model-invocation: true, which makes Claude Code request the missing argument before allowing the skill to run.

explanation: The exam guide's skill for this objective is using `argument-hint` frontmatter to prompt developers for required parameters when they invoke the skill without arguments. The other fields are real but do something else: `arguments` names positional arguments for `$name` substitution in the skill body, `when_to_use` appends invocation guidance to the skill listing, and `disable-model-invocation` controls whether Claude may load the skill at all. Divergence recorded in review-progress.md: current `skills.md` describes `argument-hint` as the hint shown during autocomplete to indicate expected arguments.

distractorNotes.a: `arguments` is a real frontmatter field: it names positional arguments so the skill body can substitute `$name`. It declares names for substitution and does not prompt for a missing value.
distractorNotes.b: `when_to_use` is a real frontmatter field: it adds invocation guidance to `description` in the skill listing. It shapes when Claude should invoke the skill, not whether an argument is supplied.
distractorNotes.d: `disable-model-invocation` prevents Claude from loading the skill automatically; it controls who invokes the skill, not whether an argument is supplied.

sourceNote: Exam Guide v1.0 § Task Statement 3.2 — argument-hint prompts developers for required parameters when a skill is invoked without arguments

stem: An architect establishes repository standards for Claude Code and must decide whether to document release procedures in the project CLAUDE.md or as a custom Skill in .claude/skills/. What architectural distinction guides this decision?

options.text: CLAUDE.md instructions are only loaded in interactive terminal sessions, whereas Skills execute exclusively in headless CI/CD pipelines.
Skills load their entire execution transcripts into context at session start, whereas CLAUDE.md instructions are deferred until referenced.
CLAUDE.md is reserved for user-specific personal shortcuts, whereas Skills provide version-controlled standards committed to the repository.
CLAUDE.md provides ambient project context loaded into every turn, whereas Skills encapsulate on-demand procedural workflows loaded only when invoked.

explanation: CLAUDE.md files provide ambient, universal instructions that load into the context window for every conversation turn (e.g., coding style, architecture invariants, build commands). Skills encapsulate procedural, task-specific workflows that are loaded on demand only when invoked (via slash commands or subagent delegation), preserving session context for routine work.

distractorNotes.a: CLAUDE.md instructions load in both interactive and headless (-p) sessions; Skills can also be invoked in both environments.
distractorNotes.b: Skills load only their names and short descriptions at session start; their full instructions load only when explicitly invoked.
distractorNotes.c: Both CLAUDE.md and Skills can be committed at the project level to establish shared repository standards.

sourceNote: Architectural distinction between ambient CLAUDE.md instructions and on-demand Skills

stem: A full-stack project has strict Terraform security policies that are completely irrelevant when editing React UI components. How can the team ensure Terraform rules load only when infrastructure files are being modified?

options.text: Create .claude/rules/terraform.md with YAML frontmatter paths: ['terraform/**/*', '**/*.tf'].
Add an exclude pattern under claudeMdExcludes in .claude/settings.json to ignore the rules during frontend file editing.
Configure a PreToolUse hook that inspects target file paths and dynamically appends Terraform policies into system context.
Add a conditional at the top of the root CLAUDE.md instructing Claude to apply the Terraform rules only when it notices it is editing infrastructure files.

explanation: Files placed in `.claude/rules/` support YAML frontmatter with a `paths` property. By specifying glob patterns (e.g. `paths: ['terraform/**/*', '**/*.tf']`), Claude Code conditionally loads the rule file into context only when files matching those paths are being inspected or edited, preserving context tokens during frontend work.

distractorNotes.b: claudeMdExcludes suppresses matching CLAUDE.md files globally across all turns, rather than conditionally loading them when editing specific files.
distractorNotes.c: Hooks execute shell scripts or validate operations, but do not provide declarative path-based memory injection; .claude/rules/ with paths frontmatter is the documented mechanism.
distractorNotes.d: A natural-language conditional in the root CLAUDE.md still loads the Terraform rules into every session and relies on the model to self-apply them; path frontmatter in a rules file loads them only when matching files are touched.

sourceNote: Using YAML frontmatter paths in .claude/rules/ to conditionally load path-scoped conventions

stem: A repository co-locates unit tests alongside implementation code across 60 separate feature directories (*.test.ts next to *.ts). The team wants strict assertion and mocking conventions enforced whenever Claude Code touches any test file, without maintaining 60 redundant instruction files or polluting context when editing non-test code. What configuration strategy best satisfies this while minimizing maintenance overhead?

options.text: Create a CLAUDE.md file in each of the 60 feature directories containing the testing rules, relying on directory-level loading to isolate them.
Define a single rule file in .claude/rules/ with frontmatter paths matching '**/*.test.ts', so conventions load automatically only when test files are touched.
Append the testing conventions to the root CLAUDE.md wrapped in an @include directive pointing to each of the 60 test file paths.
Configure a custom slash command in .claude/commands/ that developers must invoke before asking Claude Code to write or edit unit tests.

explanation: A single rule file in .claude/rules/ with a glob pattern like paths: '**/*.test.ts' centrally enforces conventions across all matching files in the project. Claude Code automatically injects the rule into context only when files matching the glob are read or edited, avoiding context bloat on unrelated edits and eliminating the burden of synchronizing 60 directory-level files.

distractorNotes.a: Maintaining 60 separate directory-level CLAUDE.md files creates massive maintenance overhead and risks configuration drift as testing conventions evolve.
distractorNotes.c: The @include directive statically inlines content into the root memory file, causing all testing rules to load into every session regardless of which files are edited.
distractorNotes.d: Requiring developers to invoke a slash command manually turns an automated convention into a manual process with non-zero human omission rate.

sourceNote: Glob-based path matching versus maintaining numerous directory-level memory files

stem: An architect is tasked with upgrading an authentication library across 45 files, which requires evaluating two competing breaking changes and establishing cross-module token refresh contracts. How should the work be initiated in Claude Code?

options.text: Begin in direct execution mode and immediately edit the core security module, letting unit tests reveal broken dependencies.
Launch a custom subagent with context: fork to execute the full refactoring immediately without creating an upfront plan.
Use plan mode to explore the codebase, assess dependencies, and establish an approved design before executing changes.
Execute the migration using headless claude -p in the background, allowing the model to autonomously commit edits across all files.

explanation: Letting Claude jump straight to coding can produce code that solves the wrong problem, so the recommended workflow uses plan mode to separate exploration from execution: explore, plan, then code. Planning is most useful when you're uncertain about the approach, when the change modifies multiple files, or when you're unfamiliar with the code being modified. A 45-file library upgrade with two competing breaking changes meets all three, so Claude should read the code and produce a plan for review before editing.

distractorNotes.a: Jumping straight into edits on an uncertain, multi-file change is what plan mode is meant to prevent; it can produce code that solves the wrong problem and needs rework.
distractorNotes.b: context: fork is a skill frontmatter field rather than a way to launch a subagent, and skipping the plan forfeits the exploration phase recommended when the approach is uncertain.
distractorNotes.d: A background -p run committing edits autonomously skips the plan-and-review step recommended when the approach is uncertain and many files change.

sourceNote: Explore first, then plan, then code - plan mode separates exploration from execution and is most useful for uncertain, multi-file changes

stem: A developer needs to fix a continuous integration test failure caused by an unhandled null value in src/utils/date.ts. The test report provides the exact line number, stack trace, and failing input. Which interaction mode in Claude Code is most efficient to resolve the issue while conserving context and latency?

options.text: Enter plan mode to perform an exploratory architectural review of the entire utility module before drafting changes.
Launch a custom Explore subagent with context: fork to isolate file searching and dependency mapping.
Turn on extended thinking with a maximum reasoning budget to perform formal verification across all date callers.
Use direct execution mode, providing the file path and stack trace so Claude Code directly inspects the line and applies the targeted fix.

explanation: When a bug is narrowly scoped, isolated to a single file, and accompanied by an explicit stack trace and failing input, direct execution mode is fastest and most context-efficient. Plan mode is designed for complex, ambiguous, multi-file changes where exploration must precede implementation.

distractorNotes.a: Plan mode introduces exploration overhead, user approval turns, and token consumption that are unnecessary for a known, localized defect with an explicit stack trace.
distractorNotes.b: An Explore subagent is intended for searching broad, unfamiliar codebases; here the file and line number are already pinpointed.
distractorNotes.c: Extended thinking increases latency and token spend without providing benefit for a routine null check fix.

sourceNote: Explore first, then plan, then code - for small, clearly scoped fixes, ask Claude to do it directly and skip the plan

stem: During a large refactoring task in Claude Code, extensive exploration of legacy source trees threatens to fill the context window with file contents. How does Claude Code's Explore subagent protect session context?

options.text: It isolates verbose file searching and reading inside a child context, returning only high-level findings to the main session.
It summarizes each file with a smaller, cheaper model and injects those summaries directly into the main session's context.
It triggers automatic context compaction after every individual file read, discarding earlier conversation turns from the main session.
It caps the main session to a fixed number of files per task, refusing to open additional files once the limit is reached.

explanation: The Explore subagent operates in an isolated context window. When tasked with locating files, patterns, or architectural relationships, it performs verbose searches and file inspections within its own window and passes only concise summaries back to the parent session, preventing main context window exhaustion.

distractorNotes.b: The protection comes from isolating the verbose reading in a separate child context and returning only findings, not from summarizing files with a cheaper model into the main session.
distractorNotes.c: Context compaction (/compact) can summarize prior turns, but the Explore subagent prevents context bloat natively by running searches in an isolated child context rather than compacting the main session after every read.
distractorNotes.d: The Explore subagent does not enforce a hard per-task file cap on the main session; it offloads verbose searching and reading into a child context and returns only high-level findings.

sourceNote: Isolating verbose codebase exploration in subagents to preserve main session context

stem: A team asks Claude Code to implement a complex date formatting function using a lengthy natural language prompt, but the generated output repeatedly fails edge cases. What is the most effective prompt engineering refinement?

options.text: Expand the prompt with an exhaustive list of negative constraints describing every forbidden date format output.
Provide concrete input and output examples that demonstrate expected transformations across tricky edge cases.
Move the lengthy specification into the system prompt so Claude weights the formatting requirements above the user-turn request.
Append general quality modifiers instructing the model to think carefully and write bug-free enterprise-grade code.

explanation: When natural language specifications are complex or ambiguous, providing concrete input/output examples (multishot prompting) is the most reliable way to clarify expected transformations and boundary behavior. Examples ground the model in exact data shapes and edge cases far more effectively than stacking negative constraints, relocating the same prose into the system prompt, or adding generic quality adjectives.

distractorNotes.a: Negative constraints ('do not do X') are harder for language models to parse consistently than positive specifications and concrete input/output demonstrations.
distractorNotes.c: Relocating the same prose does not resolve its ambiguity about edge cases; concrete input/output examples are what pin down the expected transformations.
distractorNotes.d: Vague quality modifiers and generic exhortations ('think carefully', 'write enterprise-grade code') do not provide concrete specifications for ambiguous edge cases.

sourceNote: Using concrete input/output examples to disambiguate complex transformation requirements

stem: When iterating with Claude Code to resolve a complex test suite failure, which approach enables the fastest and most accurate convergence on the fix?

options.text: Clear session context and describe the intended feature behavior in natural language without the error output.
Enter plan mode to perform an architectural review of the entire test framework before inspecting the failure.
Feed the actual test failure output and stack traces to Claude Code so it can diagnose root causes from errors.
Summarize the failure in your own words rather than pasting the raw output, so long stack traces do not crowd the context window.

explanation: Test-driven debugging in Claude Code converges fastest when the model is provided with concrete diagnostic feedback, such as terminal test outputs, stack traces, and expected-versus-actual assertion diffs. Claude Code uses these exact error details to trace code execution paths and apply targeted corrections, rather than guessing from abstract descriptions or rewriting entire modules.

distractorNotes.a: Starting over and re-describing requirements in natural language discards the precise diagnostic symptoms needed to isolate the bug.
distractorNotes.b: Entering plan mode to review the entire test framework adds conversational latency and broad exploration overhead when a concrete stack trace already isolates the bug.
distractorNotes.d: Paraphrasing discards the exact error messages, file paths and line numbers Claude needs to locate the root cause; the concrete failure output is the most useful diagnostic signal to share.

sourceNote: Feeding test failure traces to guide targeted, test-driven iterative fixes

stem: An engineer needs Claude Code to design a high-throughput caching layer for an unfamiliar domain. Which prompt pattern helps uncover architectural failure modes and design trade-offs before writing code?

options.text: The persona pattern: instruct Claude to adopt the persona of a senior cache engineer and immediately generate the implementation.
The few-shot pattern: supply code snippets from an existing Redis service and ask Claude to adapt them directly without asking questions.
Direct implementation prompt: ask Claude to produce a complete caching module from default assumptions, resolving edge cases later in testing.
The interview pattern: ask Claude to interview the engineer with clarifying questions about invalidation, consistency, and traffic patterns.

explanation: For larger features, the guidance is to have Claude interview you first: start with a minimal prompt and ask Claude to interview you using the `AskUserQuestion` tool. Claude asks about things you might not have considered yet, including technical implementation, edge cases, concerns and tradeoffs, and then writes a spec. In an unfamiliar caching domain, that surfaces invalidation, consistency and failure-mode questions before any code is written.

distractorNotes.a: A persona shapes tone and focus, but generating the implementation immediately skips questioning the engineer about unstated constraints such as invalidation rules or traffic patterns.
distractorNotes.b: Adapting existing snippets without asking questions carries over another service's assumptions and does not surface the trade-offs of an unfamiliar domain.
distractorNotes.c: Generating code from default assumptions skips requirement discovery and pushes design problems into testing, where they are more expensive to fix.

sourceNote: Let Claude interview you - have Claude interview you with AskUserQuestion to surface edge cases and tradeoffs before implementing

stem: A CI/CD pipeline step invokes Claude Code to review incoming pull requests: `claude 'Review this PR for security vulnerabilities'`. The CI build hangs indefinitely and times out. What flag is required to run Claude Code in non-interactive CI environments?

options.text: The -p (or --print) flag to run non-interactively, stream or return results to stdout, and exit cleanly.
The --daemon flag to detach the process into a background systemd unit that runs detached from the terminal session.
The --batch flag to queue the prompt into Claude Code's background worker daemon and poll for job completion.
Set a CLAUDE_NONINTERACTIVE=1 environment variable, which suppresses the interactive prompt while keeping the default REPL running.

explanation: By default, Claude Code runs as an interactive terminal application awaiting user prompts. In automated pipelines and scripts, the `-p` (or `--print`) flag runs Claude Code non-interactively in headless mode, processing the prompt, outputting the result, and exiting immediately.

distractorNotes.b: Claude Code does not use a --daemon flag for CI/CD runs.
distractorNotes.c: Claude Code does not provide a --batch flag for asynchronous worker queuing; headless runs in CI pipelines execute synchronously via -p (or --print).
distractorNotes.d: No environment variable turns the interactive REPL into a clean one-shot run; the -p/--print flag is what makes Claude Code execute non-interactively and exit.

sourceNote: Running Claude Code non-interactively in automated pipelines with the -p flag

stem: A security engineering team integrates Claude Code into an automated GitHub Actions pipeline to scan pull requests for credential leaks. The downstream CI step parses the scan findings with jq to post inline review comments. Which CLI configuration ensures the scan produces machine-readable, schema-validated JSON without freeform text or conversational envelopes?

options.text: Provide prompt instructions requesting JSON format and run with standard output redirection: claude -p '... format as json' > results.json.
Pass --output-format json combined with --json-schema defining the expected issue schema, ensuring strict structured output.
Set --output-format json on its own, which guarantees that Claude Code's response is automatically constrained to valid JSON.
Pass --output-format text and pipe the output to a Python post-processing script that extracts JSON codeblocks with regular expressions.

explanation: Running Claude Code with --output-format json and --json-schema guarantees that the output adheres strictly to the provided JSON schema without conversational preamble or markdown codeblock wrappers, enabling seamless downstream parsing with tools like jq.

distractorNotes.a: Prompting for JSON without CLI schema enforcement often results in markdown codeblocks (```json ... ```) or conversational commentary, breaking strict JSON parsers.
distractorNotes.c: --output-format json without --json-schema wraps Claude's output in a standard CLI JSON envelope, but the assistant content itself remains unstructured text unless a schema is provided.
distractorNotes.d: Regex extraction from text output is brittle and prone to breakage whenever model phrasing or error reporting variations occur.

sourceNote: Using --output-format json and --json-schema for machine-readable pipeline integrations

stem: An architect designs the configuration hierarchy for a multi-package monorepo using Claude Code. The team wants to ensure project conventions, shared standards, and team-specific instructions load predictably without bloating context or causing silent configuration overrides. According to Claude Code's memory resolution architecture, which TWO statements accurately describe how CLAUDE.md files are discovered, ordered, and loaded across the project hierarchy? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Discovered CLAUDE.md files from ancestor directories down to the working directory are concatenated into context in root-to-leaf order rather than overriding each other.
Personal preferences in CLAUDE.local.md are evaluated before project CLAUDE.md instructions at each level to ensure team standards take precedence over personal settings.
Memory files residing in subdirectories below the working directory are loaded on demand when Claude Code reads files in those directories, rather than at session launch.
Organization managed policy CLAUDE.md files can be selectively bypassed by individual repositories by specifying their absolute file paths in the claudeMdExcludes setting.
Nested subdirectory CLAUDE.md files completely shadow and discard all instructions inherited from ancestor CLAUDE.md files located in parent directories across the project tree.

explanation: In Claude Code's memory hierarchy, discovered CLAUDE.md and CLAUDE.local.md files from the filesystem root down to the current working directory are concatenated together into the context window rather than overriding or shadowing each other; ordering root-to-leaf ensures that instructions closer to where the session launched are read last. Furthermore, memory files located in subdirectories beneath the working directory are not loaded at launch to prevent context bloat; they are included on demand when Claude Code reads files in those subdirectories.

distractorNotes.b: CLAUDE.local.md is appended after CLAUDE.md within each directory level, so personal notes are the last instructions injected into context at that level rather than loading first.
distractorNotes.d: Managed policy CLAUDE.md files deployed by IT or MDM apply unconditionally across all repositories on the machine and cannot be bypassed or excluded via claudeMdExcludes.
distractorNotes.e: Claude Code concatenates ancestor memory files together rather than shadowing them; instructions from parent folders remain active alongside subdirectory instructions.

sourceNote: Concatenation hierarchy, subdirectory on-demand loading, and local override ordering

stem: An infrastructure engineer configures automated Claude Code jobs in a continuous integration (CI/CD) pipeline using headless mode (claude -p). The team wants reproducible, secure script executions that prevent untrusted repository hooks from running and avoid interactive authentication prompts. According to vendor documentation, which TWO statements accurately describe the operational and security behavior of Claude Code in this non-interactive environment? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Running claude -p without the --bare flag suspends execution and prompts the runner console for interactive workspace trust before executing repository hooks.
Passing the --bare flag skips auto-discovery of CLAUDE.md files, hooks, custom skills, and MCP servers, ensuring clean and reproducible execution in CI runners.
Background subagents spawned during a claude -p run are abruptly terminated after a 5-second grace period following completion of the primary coordinator prompt turn.
In bare mode, Claude Code never reads stored OAuth credentials or the system keychain, requiring explicit API key provisioning through environment variables.
Bare mode restricts Claude Code to executing custom slash commands while completely stripping access to the built-in Bash shell and file editing tool primitives.

explanation: When running Claude Code in non-interactive CI/CD pipelines, passing `--bare` reduces startup overhead and enforces security by skipping auto-discovery of CLAUDE.md files, hooks, skills, MCP servers, and auto memory, preventing repository configurations from introducing non-deterministic behavior. In bare mode, Claude Code never reads OAuth credentials or the system keychain, so automated runners must supply authentication via `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` (or an `apiKeyHelper` in the `--settings` JSON). Claude Code retains core file editing and Bash tools in bare mode, and while background Bash processes terminate after a 5-second grace period at exit, background subagents stay open until completion (up to a 10-minute timeout ceiling).

distractorNotes.a: Non-interactive claude -p runs never display interactive workspace trust prompts; without --bare, repository hooks in .claude/settings.json execute automatically.
distractorNotes.c: The 5-second grace period applies strictly to background Bash tasks; background subagents hold the claude -p process open until their work finishes.
distractorNotes.e: Bare mode skips custom skills and commands but maintains standard access to core primitive tools including Bash, file reading, and file editing.

sourceNote: Bare mode startup isolation, authentication requirements, and headless lifecycle management

stem: An engineer reviews a proposed refactoring generated by Claude Code for an order processing module and identifies three defects: the inventory reservation call omits a required timeout, the downstream payment client requires an idempotency key derived from the reservation ID, and the exception handler's transaction rollback references a stale variable. Because these three issues share state and lifecycle dependencies across the checkout flow, what is the recommended prompting strategy to resolve them?

options.text: Address each defect in sequential turns, starting with the reservation timeout, verifying that single change, and then prompting for the idempotency key and rollback logic in follow-up messages.
Dispatch three concurrent subagents using separate workspace worktrees to isolate each defect into a parallel branch, then merge the resulting pull requests into the feature branch.
Instruct Claude Code with a high-level directive to resolve all unhandled edge cases and transaction anomalies across the module, relying on the model to infer the state relationships.
Bundle all three defects into a single detailed prompt detailing their interdependencies, allowing Claude Code to reconcile the shared lifecycle state and apply a unified fix.

explanation: The exam guide's iterative-refinement task statement covers when to provide all issues in a single message (interacting problems) versus fixing them sequentially (independent problems). Here the timeout, the idempotency key derived from the reservation ID, and the rollback all share state across the checkout flow, so fixing them in separate turns risks each fix invalidating assumptions made in the previous one. One detailed message that spells out the interdependencies lets Claude Code reconcile the shared state in a single coherent change. Sequential iteration fits when the issues are independent.

distractorNotes.a: Sequential turn-by-turn prompts work well for independent, decoupled bugs, but when defects interact, piecemeal edits can invalidate prior fixes.
distractorNotes.b: Isolating interacting changes into independent parallel worktrees or subagents risks conflicting edits because all three defects modify shared execution flow and state.
distractorNotes.c: High-level directives lacking specific architectural context force the model to guess at the cross-service dependencies, often leading to superficial patches that fail to reconcile the shared state.

sourceNote: Exam guide Task Statement 3.5 - interacting issues go in one detailed message; independent issues are iterated sequentially

stem: An engineering team enables Code Review on its repository and wants any pull request carrying unresolved Important findings to be prevented from merging. They add the Claude Code Review check to the repository's required status checks under branch protection, but pull requests with Important findings continue to merge cleanly. What explains this behavior, and how should the team implement the merge gate?

options.text: The check run always finishes with a neutral conclusion, so branch protection cannot block on it; gating needs a separate CI step that parses the severity breakdown from the check run output.
The Claude Code Review check has to be registered as a required status check at the organization level rather than per repository before its neutral conclusion is converted into a blocking failure.
The repository must switch its Review Behavior from Once after PR creation to After every push, because only push-triggered reviews emit the pass or fail conclusion that branch protection evaluates.
The REVIEW.md severity rules must escalate the finding classes the team cares about to Important, because the check run derives its pass or fail conclusion from the highest severity it posted inline.

explanation: Code Review deliberately decouples reporting from gating. The Claude Code Review check run always completes with a neutral conclusion, which by design means it never blocks merging through branch protection rules, so adding it as a required check cannot enforce anything on its own. To gate merges on findings, the team reads the severity breakdown from the check run output in its own CI: the last line of the Details text is a machine-readable comment a workflow can parse with gh and jq, returning per-severity counts such as {"normal": 2, "nit": 1, "pre_existing": 0}. The normal key holds the count of Important findings, and a non-zero value means at least one bug is worth fixing before merge, which is the signal the workflow should fail on.

distractorNotes.b: The scope at which a check is required does not change the conclusion the check itself reports; a neutral conclusion stays neutral.
distractorNotes.c: Review Behavior controls when reviews are triggered, not what conclusion the check run reports. Every review populates the same check run with a neutral conclusion regardless of the trigger mode.
distractorNotes.d: REVIEW.md can redefine which finding classes count as Important, which changes how findings are classified and reported, but it does not alter the check run's neutral conclusion or make the check blocking.

sourceNote: Check run completes neutral and never blocks branch protection; gate merges by parsing its severity output
